About this citation

Several letters quote an earlier author — Cleanthes, Hecato, Epicurus — and in those the quoted sentence is that author's, delivered in Seneca's Latin. The archive records the inner attribution in the source field where it is known.

#### About Seneca

Lucius Annaeus Seneca (c. 4 BCE–65 CE) was a Cordoban-born Stoic, tragic playwright, and adviser—later forced suicide victim—under Nero.

### Interpretation

Seneca's claim is that everything we treat as ours — property, body, even relationships — is held on terms we do not control, whereas time is the one thing genuinely at our disposal. The argument opens the Letters and sets up the whole work's concern with how attention is spent. The claim is not that time cannot be lost but that its loss is not something done to us.

#### Why it matters

It is a piece of accounting: of the things you call yours, which can be taken without your agreement? Seneca's answer is that only one cannot.

### Questions readers arrive with

#### What is the source of the quotation “All things are alien to us; time alone…”?

“All things are alien to us; time alone…” comes from Letters to Lucilius, Ep. 1.1 (c. 62–65 CE), attributed to Seneca.

#### What does Seneca mean by time?

Is time a river, a dimension, or a structure of consciousness? Augustine, Bergson, and modern metaphysics offer rival pictures while ethics asks how finite time should be spent. This passage enters that discussion through time, love.
